Here’s how this chart works. The vertical axis is a measure of dis-similarity. The “raw” measure of dis-similarity (in this case: genetic distance) is computed pairwise between every two ancestry groups.

The tree is computed agglomeratively, merging together the two most similar pairs. The dis-similarity between two collections of ancestry groups (such as “all asians” and “all europeans”) is taken to be the average of the dis-similarities between all of their members. This is called “average linkage hierarchical clustering”.

Here is how to read it: each horizontal line corresponds to two groups. The top one here corresponds to african v non-african. This makes sense because all non-african groups are descended from a very small migrating population.

The height of the horizontal lines tells you the average dissimilarity between the ancestry groups under it. For instance there is as much genetic divergence between the asian populations in this figure as the African populations.

The pattern of merges in this figure shows that africans are far more similar among themselves (genetic distance 0.1) than they are to other groups (0.2); this is very nearly the same case for southeast asians (0.05 v 0.13) and pacific islanders (0.1 vs 0.17).

The chart does not suggest that Africans are closer to the common ancestor; only that they are furthest away from the out-of-africa groups.

In fact, as genetic distance measures the accumulation of mutations; and the human mutation rate does not appear race-specific; and the number of generations should be about the same in africa as in Europe , all the populations should be roughly the same genetic distance from the MRCA.
